title: Stars and Constellations
lead: The Bible names a few star groups: the Pleiades, Orion and the Bear. It praises God, who made the stars and counts them. It forbids worshiping them or reading the future in them. This page is about the stars as part of the natural world. The worship of the sun, moon and stars has its own page (The Host of Heaven), and so does the star the magi followed (The Magi).

sections.b:
God made the two big lights "and the stars" (Genesis 1:16). Gerhard Hasel points out that Genesis 1 does not even name the sun and moon. Their common names were also the names of gods. The chapter gives them the humble job of lights that "govern" day and night. Hasel reads this as a protest against star worship.

God "counts how many stars there are; / he calls each of them by a name" (Psalm 147:4; compare Isaiah 40:26). Abraham is told, "Look toward the sky and number the stars, if you can number them" (Genesis 15:5). Jeremiah says "the army of the heavens cannot be counted" (Jeremiah 33:22). God "has fixed the rules for the moon and stars to light the night" (Jeremiah 31:35). In poetry the stars sing at creation (Job 38:7) and fight for Israel: "The stars fought from heaven" (Judges 5:20).

sections.b:
Three star groups are named, always as God's work: "The Bear is his work, and Orion, and the Pleiades" (Job 9:9; compare Job 38:31–32; Amos 5:8). The Hebrew names are kimah, kesil and 'ash or 'ayish. The Tyndale House lexicon gives them as the Pleiades, Orion and the Great Bear; it also notes that some take 'ayish as the star Arcturus. Kesil is also the common word for "fool." Its plural, kesilim, means the constellations in general (Isaiah 13:10).

The old translators had their own guesses. The Greek of Job 9:9 has "the Pleiades and Hesperus and Arcturus." The Greek of Job 38:32 has Mazouroth and Hesperus. The Greek of Amos 5:8 names no stars at all. The KJV has "Arcturus" in Job 9:9, and "Arcturus with his sons" (Job 38:32, KJV).

God asks Job, "Can you tie the knots that hold the Pleiades, / or untie the ropes of Orion?" (Job 38:31). The KJV has "sweet influences of Pleiades" (Job 38:31, KJV). The Tyndale House lexicon gives the rare word ma'adannot as "bonds," which fits the parallel "ropes." The next verse asks about the mazzarot (Job 38:32), a word found only here. The Greek just copies it as Mazouroth, and the KJV as "Mazzaroth." The same lexicon links it with the signs of the zodiac. A similar word, mazzalot, names the "star signs" that Josiah stopped people from worshiping (2 Kings 23:5). In the Talmud, mazzal means a constellation.

The lights of the sky are "signs" for times and seasons (Genesis 1:14). But Israel was not to bow to them (Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:3) or fear them: "Do not panic at the signs in the sky, / though the nations panic at them" (Jeremiah 10:2). Isaiah mocks Babylon's experts, "the ones who map out the sky, / who stare at the stars" (Isaiah 47:13), who cannot save her. The magi of Matthew 2 did follow a star. Matthew tells it as God leading the nations to the newborn king (Matthew 2:2; Matthew 2:9–10). What the star was is discussed under The Magi.

Jewish views. The Talmud records a debate. Rabbi Yochanan taught, "There is no constellation for the Jewish people," citing Jeremiah 10:2. He tells how God led Abraham outside and told him to leave his star charts behind (compare Genesis 15:5). Rabbi Chanina held that "there is a constellation for the Jewish people" (Shabbat 156a). Maimonides ruled that a person who acts "because of an astrological calculation" is to be punished (Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship 11:9). He called such practices "falsehood and lies" (11:16).

Christian views. Basil the Great mocked horoscopes in his Hexaemeron (6.5–7). A man born under the Ram is called generous, he said, only because "such is the nature of the beast." And to blame evil on the stars is to blame "Him Who made them." In his Confessions (7.6), Augustine tells of his friend Firminius. Firminius and a slave's son were born at the same moment, under the same stars, yet lived very different lives. Twins such as Esau and Jacob show the same thing. Whatever the astrologers got right, Augustine concluded, came "not by art, but by chance." The Catechism of the Catholic Church (2116) rejects "consulting horoscopes, astrology" along with other divination. Astronomy, the study of the stars, is another matter. Calvin praised it as a study "not to be reprobated."

common: The stars are "signs" (Genesis 1:14), so they may be read for the future; Jeremiah 10:2 and Isaiah 47:13 speak against that use.
uncommon: Augustine gave up astrology after a friend told him that his father's slave was born at the same moment as he was, yet lived a very different life.
In the Talmud, Rabbi Chanina held that "there is a constellation for the Jewish people."
